blocks.text: ChatGPT 的预览功能可以把一个 HTML 代码块变成一个小型可运行网页。由于这个页面可能包含任意代码，ChatGPT 很合理地把它放在另一个网址下的受限框架中运行。预览可以执行 JavaScript，但浏览器把它当作另一个网站，因此它无法直接查看周围已登录的 ChatGPT 页面。

blocks.text: ChatGPT 的内容安全策略（CSP）又一次拦住了我们。CSP 控制页面可以加载哪些脚本，而该策略正确地拦截了内联 JavaScript。不过，它允许加载来自 YouTube 的脚本。

blocks.text: YouTube 的 oEmbed 端点支持一种 JSONP 风格的 callback 参数。JSONP 响应是 JavaScript，而不是普通 JSON。该端点试图拒绝非法的 callback，但它在返回校验错误之前，就已经把 callback 放进了响应里：

inlines.text: 关键要点
隔离的强度取决于跨越它的每一座桥。当特权监听器信任来自错误发送者的消息时，沙箱化框架仍然可能危及父页面。
postMessage

event.origin
和
event.source
HTML 注入可以通过一个全新的、未沙箱化的文档和一个允许的第三方脚本端点，变成 JavaScript 执行。CSP 是有价值的纵深防御，但它无法让不安全的渲染路径变得安全。
同源 JavaScript 的影响必须在受害者的已认证上下文中衡量。一旦代码以
chatgpt.com
身份运行，它就能访问正常前端可访问的相同私有数据和账户操作——而不仅仅是弹出一个警告框。
跨功能测试很重要。这条攻击链存在于公共分享、Preview、MathLive、框架创建和 CSP 之间的接缝中，而不是在单独查看的任何一个功能中。

blocks.text: 更广泛的教训是，安全边界必须在整个产品中成立，而不仅仅是在单个组件内部。任何公开或可分享的表面都应被视为攻击者控制的输入，每条跨框架消息都应经过身份验证，不受信任的标记应在整个渲染路径中保持沙箱化。

blocks.text: It started with a graph and a Preview

blocks.text: The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

inlines.text: The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

blocks.text: ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

blocks.text: At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

blocks.text: The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

blocks.text: Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

blocks.text: MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

blocks.text: ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

blocks.text: YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

blocks.text: What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

inlines.text: What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

blocks.text: The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

inlines.text: The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

blocks.text: Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

inlines.text: Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:
MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the
chatgpt.com
identity.

blocks.text: The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

inlines.text: The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

blocks.text: OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

blocks.text: The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

inlines.text: The defensive lessons are fairly simple:
A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission.
Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML.
Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame.
CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.

blocks.text: This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.

blocks.text: Key takeaways

inlines.text: Key takeaways
Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender.
postMessage
receivers must authenticate both
event.origin
and
event.source
before accepting state-changing instructions.

HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe.
The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as
chatgpt.com
, it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert.
Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone.

blocks.text: The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.
